## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The story management tells has moved, deliberately and in a straight line, from "we have stopped the bleeding" to "we are now a profitable, scalable platform."

The subtext was a company still proving it could be consistently profitable after a 2021-2022 regulatory crisis that saw centers sanctioned and enrollment frozen.

By the September 2025 year-end call, the tone turned to delivery: "Fiscal 2025 was a year of delivery. We made clear commitments, and we followed through." Full-year adjusted EBITDA of $34.5 million beat the high end of guidance, and management issued fiscal-2026 guidance for $56-65 million — implying it expected to nearly double profit again.

By February 2026 (fiscal second quarter 2026), the headline was that the company had already hit its multi-year margin target early: a 9.2% adjusted EBITDA margin, "for the first time," against an Investor-Day goal of 8-9% over a two-to-four-year horizon. First-half EBITDA of $39.8 million had already exceeded all of fiscal 2025.

By the May 2026 call, guidance had been raised twice and now sits at $85-90 million of adjusted EBITDA on $950-975 million of revenue. The new emphasis is forward-looking growth (de novo centers in Florida, a Tampa General Hospital partnership, AI-enabled scheduling, and "PACE-inspired adjacencies") plus a clear, repeated caution about the fiscal-2027 rate environment.

Growth drivers introduced over the arc: in-sourcing of pharmacy and hospice (a cost lever), hospital joint ventures (Orlando Health, then Tampa General), and an AI/efficiency program. Drivers quietly de-emphasized: the early "de novo loss" hand-wringing of 2025 has faded as those centers matured, and the census-growth story was softened on purpose — management chose to disenroll members who had lost Medicaid eligibility, trading top-line growth for margin.

# InnovAge Holding Corp. (INNV) — Forensic Dossier

*Interrogator note: this covers six consecutive earnings calls, from the fiscal third quarter of 2025 (reported May 2025) through the fiscal third quarter of 2026 (reported May 2026). InnovAge runs PACE — the Program of All-inclusive Care for the Elderly — a fully-capitated model that receives a fixed monthly payment from Medicare and Medicaid to cover all care for frail, mostly dual-eligible seniors. It is the largest PACE operator in the country by census: roughly 8,050 participants across 20 centers in six states.*

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The story evolved in three clean stages, and management narrated the transition honestly at each step.

**Stage one — stabilization (early 2025).** In the May 2025 call, the framing was recovery from a troubled past: coming off regulatory sanctions and enrollment freezes, the emphasis was on "operational stabilization," medical-cost discipline, and clearing a California enrollment backlog. Adjusted EBITDA (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization, a rough cash-earnings proxy) was a thin $10.8M that quarter, and guidance for full fiscal 2025 was modest.

**Stage two — transformation (mid-to-late 2025).** By the September 2025 year-end call the language shifted from "stabilization" to "enterprise transformation." Management delivered fiscal 2025 adjusted EBITDA of $34.5M — above the top of its own $31M guide — and then issued a striking fiscal 2026 guide of $56–65M, implying a near-doubling. The five-pillar operating framework, in-sourcing of pharmacy and hospice, and the Epic medical-records rollout became the growth drivers.

**Stage three — margin victory and a pivot to growth (early-to-mid 2026).** By February 2026 the company reported a 9.2% adjusted-EBITDA margin — hitting, for the first time, the 8–9% intermediate target it had set two years earlier at its Investor Day, and hitting it years ahead of schedule. By the May 2026 call, management said it had "pulled forward into two years what we thought was going to take three," achieved positive net income for the first time since 2021, and — critically — reoriented the narrative from margin expansion to reinvestment in growth and quality. Full-year fiscal 2026 adjusted-EBITDA guidance was raised twice, ending at $85–90M — more than 2.5x the original $34.5M base.

The one growth driver introduced late and worth watching: artificial-intelligence pilots in scheduling, care coordination and clinical workflows, plus a policy push for a "Medicare-only" PACE pathway to widen the eligible population. Both are early-stage optionality, not current earnings.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim | The hard numbers | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Adjusted EBITDA more than doubled over two fiscal years" | $34.5M FY25 vs ~$87.5M FY26 guide midpoint; H1-FY26 alone ($39.8M) already exceeded all of FY25 | **Matches — and then some.** The cash-earnings ramp is real and corroborated. |
| "Margins expanding" | Center-level contribution margin 17.3% → 18% → high-teens; adjusted-EBITDA margin ~4% FY25 → 9.2% in the December 2025 quarter | **Matches.** Genuine, fast margin expansion. |
| "Achieved positive net income for the first time since 2021" | True for the September 2025 quarter — but full-year net income is still negative (FY25 net loss ~$30M; trailing diluted EPS −$0.30; the March-2026 quarter still printed a GAAP loss of ~$0.22, missing the −$0.06 consensus) | **Richer than the trajectory justifies.** Adjusted EBITDA is soaring; GAAP profit and free cash flow are barely breaking even. |
| "Strong, durable momentum" | Revenue $854M FY25 (+11.8%); FY26 guide $950–975M. But trailing free cash flow is only ~$39M on a ~$1.56B market value — roughly 40x, and price-to-free-cash-flow screens at 58.6x | **Partly.** Top-line growth is durable; the cash-conversion story is not yet there. This is a capital-intensive, full-risk model. |
| "FY26 upside is operational, not one-time" | Management's own May 2026 words undercut this: results "supported by several in-year factors that came in more favorably than we expected, including better-than-expected Medicaid rates and favorable Medicare risk scores" | **This is the crack.** Some of the beat is rate/risk-score luck they concede won't repeat. |

The core tension: the operating turnaround is verified and impressive, but the market value now rests on adjusted EBITDA that management itself says was flattered by favorable, non-repeating reimbursement dynamics — while GAAP earnings and cash flow lag far behind.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Rising, steadily and credibly.** May 2025: cautious, "disciplined," recovery-flavored ("we know what we need to do and we're doing it"). September 2025: confident enough to guide to a near-doubling of earnings. February 2026: declaratively victorious — "for the first time, we achieved that target." May 2026: confident but, notably, adding a deliberate note of caution about fiscal 2027 ("we are also being thoughtful about our assumptions as we look ahead to fiscal 2027"). The shift from offensive (margin expansion) to a blended posture (reinvest in growth/quality, guard against a tougher rate year) is the tell that management sees the easy margin gains as banked and the next leg as harder.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**High.** This is the strongest part of the file. FY25 adjusted EBITDA beat the top of guidance ($34.5M vs $31M ceiling). FY26 guidance was raised twice within the year ($56–65M in September → $85–90M by May). Each raise was backed by delivered quarters, not promises. The screener's 57% earnings-beat rate understates the operational reliability because the misses are GAAP-EPS misses (still loss-making) while the adjusted-EBITDA and revenue guide has been beaten consistently. There is a mild sandbagging pattern on the Q4 setup (the CFO repeatedly declines to signal where within guidance they will land, citing "true-up" variability). Reliability: **High** on the operating metrics that management steers to.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

Analysts pushed hardest on three recurring themes, and management's answers were candid but incomplete:
- **De novo (new-center) losses.** Goldman pressed on the path to breakeven in Florida (Orlando/Tampa) and Los Angeles (Crenshaw); management guided losses of $13.4–15.4M for FY26 and admitted "some variability on the cost side" (transportation in Florida). Still a drag, not yet a contributor.
- **Cost-of-care step-ups.** Analysts flagged cost of care rising faster than revenue; management attributed it to in-sourcing pharmacy and hospice ("a one-time step-up… you'll see a more normalized growth rate going forward") and to income-statement "geography" that muddies quarter-over-quarter reads. - **Fiscal 2027 rate environment.** JPMorgan and others probed the CMS calendar-year-2027 Medicare Advantage advance notice (which drives PACE payment) and the accelerated blended risk-score transition. Management deferred detail to the September 2026 guidance and would not quantify the headwind — the single biggest unaddressed worry.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🟢 Adjusted EBITDA more than doubled in two years and hit the 8–9% margin target years early — verified against the numbers.
🟢 Balance sheet is clean: net cash of roughly $45M (cash ~$139M against ~$94M of debt including leases), a genuine positive.
🟢 Census growing ~10% a year; medical-cost management outperforming peers during a heavy-utilization ("quad-demic") period.
🟢 Insider open-market activity modestly net-buying (11 buys vs 13 sells, but more shares bought than sold) — a mild positive-conviction signal once grant noise is stripped out.
🔴 Heavy C-suite turnover through the turnaround: the Chief Medical Officer left (May 2025), a new one arrived (November 2025); the President/COO Michael Scarbrough departed "for personal reasons" (announced October 2025), replaced by Jennifer Browne (effective June 2026); new Chief Administrative Officer and an expanded Chief Growth Officer. Four-plus senior seats changed hands in a year.
🔴 Management concedes the fiscal-2026 beat was partly favorable, non-repeating Medicaid rates and Medicare risk scores.
🔴 100% dependence on a single payer source — government reimbursement — into a period of legislated Medicaid cuts (the reconciliation law), redeterminations, and an accelerating CMS risk-model transition for calendar 2027.
🔴 The stock has already re-rated roughly 3.5x off its 52-week low ($3.13 to ~$11.5) and sits near the top of its range; the sell-side price target (~$6.80) is about 40% *below* the current price.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

- The vocabulary migrated from "stabilization" (2025) to "transformation" to, by May 2026, "a more forward-looking view on growth" and "strategic flexibility" — language that usually precedes capital deployment (de novo centers, M&A, adjacencies). The CEO explicitly said expanding margins further is now a lower priority than "investing in growth while maintaining a consistent margin." Translation: the margin tailwind is largely spent; future upside must come from volume and new products, which are lower-certainty.
- Repeated, escalating references to "recent legislation and federal budget cuts" in the forward-looking-statements preamble across successive calls — a quiet acknowledgement that the policy backdrop is the dominant swing factor.
- The AI narrative appeared only in the last two calls and is carefully hedged ("early days," "test, learn, measure") — optionality being seeded, not a driver.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: STRENGTHENING operationally — but the re-rating is spent.** This is a genuine, well-executed turnaround where management said what it would do and did it. The problem for a capital allocator is not the business; it is the price. The stock has already captured the turnaround, trades above where the sell-side values it, and rests on adjusted earnings that management itself flagged as flattered by non-repeating reimbursement luck heading into a tougher fiscal-2027 rate year.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing:** the fiscal-2027 guidance due in September 2026. That is when the favorable Medicaid-rate and Medicare-risk-score tailwinds normalize and the calendar-2027 CMS risk-model change bites. A guide that shows margin give-back would puncture a multiple built on continued beats. There is little margin of safety and no structural floor beneath the current price (net cash is only ~$0.33/share; centers are leased).

**Moat:** a narrow, regulatory-license moat — PACE program approvals, state contracts, and the operating scale to manage medical cost are real barriers, but InnovAge is subscale against the managed-care giants and has no pricing power: rates are set by the government. **Moat trend: stable** — operations are improving fast, but returns on capital are still negative (return on invested capital about −1.5%) and the durability of the earnings base depends on payers InnovAge does not control. **Secular threat: material (not terminal)** — reimbursement compression (Medicaid directed-payment and eligibility cuts, the calendar-2027 Medicare risk-model transition, provider-tax and subsidy pressure) is a real, dated headwind to the whole capitated-senior-care cohort. It is not terminal because PACE is a structurally favored, low-total-cost model that policymakers are inclined to expand, not shrink — but the cheapness here is not the issue; the stock is not cheap.

# InnovAge Holding Corp. (INNV) — Forensic Dossier

*Interrogator note: this covers six consecutive earnings calls, from the fiscal third quarter of 2025 (reported May 2025) through the fiscal third quarter of 2026 (reported May 2026). InnovAge runs PACE — the Program of All-inclusive Care for the Elderly — a fully-capitated model that receives a fixed monthly payment from Medicare and Medicaid to cover all care for frail, mostly dual-eligible seniors. It is the largest PACE operator in the country by census: roughly 8,050 participants across 20 centers in six states.*

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The story evolved in three clean stages, and management narrated the transition honestly at each step.

**Stage one — stabilization (early 2025).** In the May 2025 call, the framing was recovery from a troubled past: coming off regulatory sanctions and enrollment freezes, the emphasis was on "operational stabilization," medical-cost discipline, and clearing a California enrollment backlog. Adjusted EBITDA (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization, a rough cash-earnings proxy) was a thin $10.8M that quarter, and guidance for full fiscal 2025 was modest.

**Stage two — transformation (mid-to-late 2025).** By the September 2025 year-end call the language shifted from "stabilization" to "enterprise transformation." Management delivered fiscal 2025 adjusted EBITDA of $34.5M — above the top of its own $31M guide — and then issued a striking fiscal 2026 guide of $56–65M, implying a near-doubling. The five-pillar operating framework, in-sourcing of pharmacy and hospice, and the Epic medical-records rollout became the growth drivers.

**Stage three — margin victory and a pivot to growth (early-to-mid 2026).** By February 2026 the company reported a 9.2% adjusted-EBITDA margin — hitting, for the first time, the 8–9% intermediate target it had set two years earlier at its Investor Day, and hitting it years ahead of schedule. By the May 2026 call, management said it had "pulled forward into two years what we thought was going to take three," achieved positive net income for the first time since 2021, and — critically — reoriented the narrative from margin expansion to reinvestment in growth and quality. Full-year fiscal 2026 adjusted-EBITDA guidance was raised twice, ending at $85–90M — more than 2.5x the original $34.5M base.

The one growth driver introduced late and worth watching: artificial-intelligence pilots in scheduling, care coordination and clinical workflows, plus a policy push for a "Medicare-only" PACE pathway to widen the eligible population. Both are early-stage optionality, not current earnings.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim | The hard numbers | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Adjusted EBITDA more than doubled over two fiscal years" | $34.5M FY25 vs ~$87.5M FY26 guide midpoint; H1-FY26 alone ($39.8M) already exceeded all of FY25 | **Matches — and then some.** The cash-earnings ramp is real and corroborated. |
| "Margins expanding" | Center-level contribution margin 17.3% → 18% → high-teens; adjusted-EBITDA margin ~4% FY25 → 9.2% in the December 2025 quarter | **Matches.** Genuine, fast margin expansion. |
| "Achieved positive net income for the first time since 2021" | True for the September 2025 quarter — but full-year net income is still negative (FY25 net loss ~$30M; trailing diluted EPS −$0.30; the March-2026 quarter still printed a GAAP loss of ~$0.22, missing the −$0.06 consensus) | **Richer than the trajectory justifies.** Adjusted EBITDA is soaring; GAAP profit and free cash flow are barely breaking even. |
| "Strong, durable momentum" | Revenue $854M FY25 (+11.8%); FY26 guide $950–975M. But trailing free cash flow is only ~$39M on a ~$1.56B market value — roughly 40x, and price-to-free-cash-flow screens at 58.6x | **Partly.** Top-line growth is durable; the cash-conversion story is not yet there. This is a capital-intensive, full-risk model. |
| "FY26 upside is operational, not one-time" | Management's own May 2026 words undercut this: results "supported by several in-year factors that came in more favorably than we expected, including better-than-expected Medicaid rates and favorable Medicare risk scores" | **This is the crack.** Some of the beat is rate/risk-score luck they concede won't repeat. |

The core tension: the operating turnaround is verified and impressive, but the market value now rests on adjusted EBITDA that management itself says was flattered by favorable, non-repeating reimbursement dynamics — while GAAP earnings and cash flow lag far behind.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Rising, steadily and credibly.** May 2025: cautious, "disciplined," recovery-flavored ("we know what we need to do and we're doing it"). September 2025: confident enough to guide to a near-doubling of earnings. February 2026: declaratively victorious — "for the first time, we achieved that target." May 2026: confident but, notably, adding a deliberate note of caution about fiscal 2027 ("we are also being thoughtful about our assumptions as we look ahead to fiscal 2027"). The shift from offensive (margin expansion) to a blended posture (reinvest in growth/quality, guard against a tougher rate year) is the tell that management sees the easy margin gains as banked and the next leg as harder.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**High.** This is the strongest part of the file. FY25 adjusted EBITDA beat the top of guidance ($34.5M vs $31M ceiling). FY26 guidance was raised twice within the year ($56–65M in September → $85–90M by May). Each raise was backed by delivered quarters, not promises. The screener's 57% earnings-beat rate understates the operational reliability because the misses are GAAP-EPS misses (still loss-making) while the adjusted-EBITDA and revenue guide has been beaten consistently. There is a mild sandbagging pattern on the Q4 setup (the CFO repeatedly declines to signal where within guidance they will land, citing "true-up" variability). Reliability: **High** on the operating metrics that management steers to.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

Analysts pushed hardest on three recurring themes, and management's answers were candid but incomplete:
- **De novo (new-center) losses.** Goldman pressed on the path to breakeven in Florida (Orlando/Tampa) and Los Angeles (Crenshaw); management guided losses of $13.4–15.4M for FY26 and admitted "some variability on the cost side" (transportation in Florida). Still a drag, not yet a contributor.
- **Cost-of-care step-ups.** Analysts flagged cost of care rising faster than revenue; management attributed it to in-sourcing pharmacy and hospice ("a one-time step-up… you'll see a more normalized growth rate going forward") and to income-statement "geography" that muddies quarter-over-quarter reads. Plausible, but it asks investors to trust adjustments they cannot independently verify.
- **Fiscal 2027 rate environment.** JPMorgan and others probed the CMS calendar-year-2027 Medicare Advantage advance notice (which drives PACE payment) and the accelerated blended risk-score transition. Management deferred detail to the September 2026 guidance and would not quantify the headwind — the single biggest unaddressed worry.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🟢 Adjusted EBITDA more than doubled in two years and hit the 8–9% margin target years early — verified against the numbers.
🟢 Balance sheet is clean: net cash of roughly $45M (cash ~$139M against ~$94M of debt including leases), a genuine positive.
🟢 Census growing ~10% a year; medical-cost management outperforming peers during a heavy-utilization ("quad-demic") period.
🟢 Insider open-market activity modestly net-buying (11 buys vs 13 sells, but more shares bought than sold) — a mild positive-conviction signal once grant noise is stripped out.
🔴 Heavy C-suite turnover through the turnaround: the Chief Medical Officer left (May 2025), a new one arrived (November 2025); the President/COO Michael Scarbrough departed "for personal reasons" (announced October 2025), replaced by Jennifer Browne (effective June 2026); new Chief Administrative Officer and an expanded Chief Growth Officer. Four-plus senior seats changed hands in a year.
🔴 Management concedes the fiscal-2026 beat was partly favorable, non-repeating Medicaid rates and Medicare risk scores.
🔴 100% dependence on a single payer source — government reimbursement — into a period of legislated Medicaid cuts (the reconciliation law), redeterminations, and an accelerating CMS risk-model transition for calendar 2027.
🔴 The stock has already re-rated roughly 3.5x off its 52-week low ($3.13 to ~$11.5) and sits near the top of its range; the sell-side price target (~$6.80) is about 40% *below* the current price.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

- The vocabulary migrated from "stabilization" (2025) to "transformation" to, by May 2026, "a more forward-looking view on growth" and "strategic flexibility" — language that usually precedes capital deployment (de novo centers, M&A, adjacencies). The CEO explicitly said expanding margins further is now a lower priority than "investing in growth while maintaining a consistent margin." Translation: the margin tailwind is largely spent; future upside must come from volume and new products, which are lower-certainty.
- Repeated, escalating references to "recent legislation and federal budget cuts" in the forward-looking-statements preamble across successive calls — a quiet acknowledgement that the policy backdrop is the dominant swing factor.
- The AI narrative appeared only in the last two calls and is carefully hedged ("early days," "test, learn, measure") — optionality being seeded, not a driver.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: STRENGTHENING operationally — but the re-rating is spent.** This is a genuine, well-executed turnaround where management said what it would do and did it. The problem for a capital allocator is not the business; it is the price. The stock has already captured the turnaround, trades above where the sell-side values it, and rests on adjusted earnings that management itself flagged as flattered by non-repeating reimbursement luck heading into a tougher fiscal-2027 rate year.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing:** the fiscal-2027 guidance due in September 2026. That is when the favorable Medicaid-rate and Medicare-risk-score tailwinds normalize and the calendar-2027 CMS risk-model change bites. A guide that shows margin give-back would puncture a multiple built on continued beats. There is little margin of safety and no structural floor beneath the current price (net cash is only ~$0.33/share; centers are leased).

**Moat:** a narrow, regulatory-license moat — PACE program approvals, state contracts, and the operating scale to manage medical cost are real barriers, but InnovAge is subscale against the managed-care giants and has no pricing power: rates are set by the government. **Moat trend: stable** — operations are improving fast, but returns on capital are still negative (return on invested capital about −1.5%) and the durability of the earnings base depends on payers InnovAge does not control. **Secular threat: material (not terminal)** — reimbursement compression (Medicaid directed-payment and eligibility cuts, the calendar-2027 Medicare risk-model transition, provider-tax and subsidy pressure) is a real, dated headwind to the whole capitated-senior-care cohort. It is not terminal because PACE is a structurally favored, low-total-cost model that policymakers are inclined to expand, not shrink — but the cheapness here is not the issue; the stock is not cheap.

CREDIBILITY_SCORE: 4 | TRAJECTORY: STRENGTHENING | MOAT: NARROW | MOAT_TREND: STABLE | SECULAR_THREAT: material

# InnovAge Holding Corp (INNV) — A Deep Dive on Management and the Setup

*Forensic dossier prepared for the investment committee. InnovAge is the largest provider in the United States of PACE (the Program of All-Inclusive Care for the Elderly — a fully government-funded model that lets frail, mostly dual-eligible seniors stay in their homes instead of a nursing facility). Roughly 8,050 participants across 20 centers in 6 states. Transcripts span five consecutive quarters, from the fiscal third quarter of 2025 (reported May 2025) through the fiscal third quarter of 2026 (reported May 2026). The company's fiscal year ends June 30.*

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The story evolves cleanly from "stabilize and survive" to "we have turned the corner, now we grow." That arc is unusually linear and, importantly, it is corroborated by the numbers rather than contradicted by them.

- **May 2025 (fiscal Q3'25):** the tone is one of a company still proving it can operate. Management stresses discipline, "operational stabilization to enterprise transformation," and mitigating churn during Medicare open-enrollment season. Adjusted EBITDA (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization, adjusted for one-offs) is a thin $10.8 million (a 4.9% margin), described as "more than 3.5 times" the prior-year quarter — i.e., recovering off a very low base.
- **September 2025 (fiscal Q4'25 / full year):** the pivot to confidence. Full-year adjusted EBITDA of $34.5 million came in "above the high end" of guidance. Management explicitly ties results back to commitments made at a February 2024 investor day and claims it delivered on each. Fiscal 2026 guidance is introduced at $56–65 million of adjusted EBITDA — already a near-doubling.
- **November 2025 (fiscal Q1'26):** the inflection is named out loud — "positive net income this quarter for the first time since 2021." Revenue up 15% year over year, adjusted EBITDA "more than doubled."
- **February 2026 (fiscal Q2'26):** the long-term margin target is hit years early — a 9.2% adjusted EBITDA margin, versus an 8–9% goal management had framed as a "two-to-four-year" journey. First-half adjusted EBITDA of $39.8 million already exceeded the entire prior fiscal year.
- **May 2026 (fiscal Q3'26):** full-year guidance is raised again to $85–90 million of adjusted EBITDA (from the original $56–65 million), and the language shifts to a "forward-looking view on growth," strategic flexibility, and even PACE-adjacent new products.

New growth drivers introduced along the way: hospital joint ventures (Orlando Health, then Tampa General), in-sourcing of pharmacy and hospice, and — most recently — artificial-intelligence pilots for scheduling and care coordination. A driver quietly de-emphasized: further margin expansion. By May 2026 management is explicit that it now prefers "investing in growth while maintaining a consistent margin" over pushing margins higher.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim | The numbers | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Positive net income for the first time since 2021" (Q1'26) | Fiscal-year net income was negative every year 2021–2025 (−$44M, −$7M, −$41M, −$21M, −$30M); quarterly net income turned positive Q1'26 and was +$11.8M in Q2'26 | Holds up — a genuine inflection, though trailing-twelve-month earnings per share is still slightly negative (−$0.30) because earlier weak quarters remain in the window |
| Adjusted EBITDA "more than doubled" and guidance raised repeatedly | FY25 adjusted EBITDA $34.5M → H1'26 alone $39.8M → FY26 guide lifted to $85–90M | Holds up, and then some — the raise from $56–65M to $85–90M mid-year is the single most important fact in the file |
| Revenue "greater than 10% compound annual growth" | Revenue 2021→2025: $638M, $699M, $688M, $764M, $854M; Q3'26 run-rate ~$1.0B | Holds up — steady double-digit top-line growth |
| Strong medical-cost control "while others face pressure" | Center-level contribution margin expanded 17.3% → 18%+; per-participant medical spend declined sequentially in multiple quarters | Holds up — the integrated model does appear to be managing cost trend better than typical managed-care peers |
| The 8–9% margin target, framed as multi-year | Hit 9.2% in Q2'26, well ahead of schedule | Over-delivered |

Where the story is *richer than the numbers justify*: earnings quality. Management itself concedes fiscal 2026 was helped by "several in-year factors that came in more favorably than we expected, including better-than-expected Medicaid rates and favorable Medicare risk scores" (Q3'26). So a meaningful slice of the beat is a favorable rate cycle, not pure self-help — and rate cycles reverse. The full-year guide of $85–90M also implies a sharp fourth-quarter step-down (roughly $15–20M) after a $30M third quarter, which management attributes to seasonal true-ups but which flatters the third-quarter optics. In-sourcing pharmacy also moved costs around the income statement ("geography"), making clean quarter-over-quarter comparison harder.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Rising, steadily and credibly.** The progression is textbook: from defensive ("disciplined," "stabilization," "mitigating churn") in May 2025 to offensive ("strategic flexibility," "forward-looking view on growth," "PACE-inspired adjacencies") by May 2026.

- May 2025: "we know what we need to do and we're doing it, steadily and consistently" — measured, almost cautious.
- September 2025: "Fiscal 2025 was a year of delivery. We made clear commitments, and we followed through."
- February 2026: hitting the 9.2% margin target "for the first time" — visible pride.
- May 2026: "our momentum … is real and increasingly durable" — the most confident language in the set, but paired with a deliberate hedge about fiscal 2027.

Guidance became *more* specific over time (precise census, member-month, revenue and de-novo-loss ranges), which is a mark of confidence, not evasion.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**High.** This is the strongest single element of the file. Management set fiscal 2025 adjusted EBITDA guidance and beat the high end ($34.5M vs a $31M cap). It then set fiscal 2026 guidance conservatively and raised it twice, materially, as the year unfolded. The screener's earnings-beat rate (4 of 7 quarters, 57%) understates the recent pattern because it includes the older, pre-turnaround misses; the last several quarters are a clean string of meet-or-beat. There is a mild sandbagging signature — the fourth-quarter implied step-down and the repeated "we're being thoughtful about our assumptions" hedge suggest management prefers to guide low and raise. Reliability: high.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

Analysts (Goldman Sachs' Jamie Perse, JPMorgan's Benjamin Rossi, and others) pushed hardest on three recurring themes:

1. **De-novo (brand-new center) losses** — repeatedly probed on timing to break-even for the Florida centers; management stayed vague ("we'll put out some guidance"), and the fiscal 2026 de-novo-loss guide of $13.4–15.4M confirms these are still a real drag.
2. **Cost-of-care step-ups** — a 19.7% sequential jump in one quarter drew scrutiny; management attributed it to pharmacy in-sourcing and one-time items, asking analysts to "tease that out." Plausible, but it relies on the committee taking management's word on the underlying "low single digits" core trend.
3. **The fiscal 2027 rate environment** — the most important unanswered question. Management would not quantify the impact of the CMS (Medicare's regulator) advance notice for calendar-year 2027, which proposes a blended risk-score model (50% of the older 2017 model, 50% of the proposed 2027 model) plus coding-intensity and fee-for-service normalization changes. Management deferred to the September 2026 guidance call. This is the topic most likely to turn into bad news.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🟢 A real earnings inflection: first positive net income since 2021, margin target hit years early, guidance raised twice.
🟢 A clean balance sheet: net cash of roughly $45 million (about $139M cash against $94M of debt including leases), so no solvency or maturity-wall risk.
🟢 No material compliance deficiencies reported for fiscal 2025 — meaningful for a company that was under a CMS enrollment sanction in 2021.
🟢 Genuine cost-trend outperformance versus managed-care peers, driven by the integrated in-center model.

🔴 Heavy C-suite churn during the "transformation": the Chief Medical Officer left (May 2025), a new one arrived (November 2025), and the President/Chief Operating Officer, Michael Scarbrough, departed for "personal reasons" (announced October 2025) barely a year into leading the turnaround — a lot of turnover at the top for a company claiming stability.
🔴 Earnings quality: management's own admission that favorable Medicaid rates and Medicare risk scores boosted fiscal 2026 means part of the beat is cyclical, not structural.
🔴 One hundred percent government-funded revenue (Medicare plus Medicaid), so the entire earnings base is exposed to a single, unpredictable driver — reimbursement rates — with federal budget pressure a live theme in every call's cautionary language.

By the September 2025 year-end call, the tone turned to delivery: "Fiscal 2025 was a year of delivery. We made clear commitments, and we followed through." Full-year adjusted EBITDA of $34.5 million beat the high end of guidance, and management issued fiscal-2026 guidance for $56-65 million — implying it expected to nearly double profit again.

By February 2026 (fiscal second quarter 2026), the headline was that the company had already hit its multi-year margin target early: a 9.2% adjusted EBITDA margin, "for the first time," against an Investor-Day goal of 8-9% over a two-to-four-year horizon. First-half EBITDA of $39.8 million had already exceeded all of fiscal 2025.

By the May 2026 call, guidance had been raised twice and now sits at $85-90 million of adjusted EBITDA on $950-975 million of revenue. The new emphasis is forward-looking growth (de novo centers in Florida, a Tampa General Hospital partnership, AI-enabled scheduling, and "PACE-inspired adjacencies") plus a clear, repeated caution about the fiscal-2027 rate environment.

Growth drivers introduced over the arc: in-sourcing of pharmacy and hospice (a cost lever), hospital joint ventures (Orlando Health, then Tampa General), and an AI/efficiency program. Drivers quietly de-emphasized: the early "de novo loss" hand-wringing of 2025 has faded as those centers matured, and the census-growth story was softened on purpose — management chose to disenroll members who had lost Medicaid eligibility, trading top-line growth for margin.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim | What the financials show | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Adjusted EBITDA more than doubled… achieved 8-9% margin target" (Feb 2026) | Revenue grew to $854M in fiscal 2025 (+11.8%); web-verified Q3-FY26 adjusted EBITDA $30.5M; the operating improvement is real | Matches — the operating turnaround is genuine |
| "Achieved positive net income… for the first time since 2021" (Nov 2025) | The multi-year trajectory is five straight net losses: -$44M (2021), -$7M, -$41M, -$21M, -$30M (2025). GAAP net margin -3.6%, return on equity -10.2%, return on invested capital -1.5% | Richer than the numbers — one clean quarter does not undo five years of GAAP losses; trailing diluted EPS is still -$0.30 |

The most important divergence is not operational, it is on the bottom line and the price. 1. **Cost-of-care "geography."** Management has had to explain, call after call, that in-sourcing pharmacy and hospice shifts expenses between income-statement lines, making quarter-over-quarter cost trends look worse than the underlying. **Trajectory: STRENGTHENING operationally — but the value question is about price and terminal reimbursement, not execution.**

# InnovAge Holding (INNV) — A deep dive on management and the setup

*Forensic dossier prepared for the investment committee. Source material: five consecutive InnovAge earnings calls (May 2025 through May 2026) cross-referenced against the screener's hard financials. InnovAge is the largest U.S. operator of PACE centers — the Program of All-inclusive Care for the Elderly, a fully-capitated managed-care model that is paid a fixed monthly amount per frail senior by Medicaid and Medicare to deliver all of that person's health care, taking the full risk of that care.*

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The story management tells has moved, deliberately and in a straight line, from "we have stopped the bleeding" to "we are now a profitable, scalable platform."

In the May 2025 call (fiscal third quarter 2025), the framing was stabilization-with-early-momentum: chief executive Patrick Blair described a shift "from operational stabilization to enterprise transformation," with adjusted EBITDA (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization — a rough proxy for operating cash profit) of just $10.8 million on a 4.9% margin. The subtext was a company still proving it could be consistently profitable after a 2021-2022 regulatory crisis that saw centers sanctioned and enrollment frozen.

By the September 2025 year-end call, the tone turned to delivery: "Fiscal 2025 was a year of delivery. We made clear commitments, and we followed through." Full-year adjusted EBITDA of $34.5 million beat the high end of guidance, and management issued fiscal-2026 guidance for $56-65 million — implying it expected to nearly double profit again.

By February 2026 (fiscal second quarter 2026), the headline was that the company had already hit its multi-year margin target early: a 9.2% adjusted EBITDA margin, "for the first time," against an Investor-Day goal of 8-9% over a two-to-four-year horizon. First-half EBITDA of $39.8 million had already exceeded all of fiscal 2025.

By the May 2026 call, guidance had been raised twice and now sits at $85-90 million of adjusted EBITDA on $950-975 million of revenue. The new emphasis is forward-looking growth (de novo centers in Florida, a Tampa General Hospital partnership, AI-enabled scheduling, and "PACE-inspired adjacencies") plus a clear, repeated caution about the fiscal-2027 rate environment.

Growth drivers introduced over the arc: in-sourcing of pharmacy and hospice (a cost lever), hospital joint ventures (Orlando Health, then Tampa General), and an AI/efficiency program. Drivers quietly de-emphasized: the early "de novo loss" hand-wringing of 2025 has faded as those centers matured, and the census-growth story was softened on purpose — management chose to disenroll members who had lost Medicaid eligibility, trading top-line growth for margin.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim | What the financials show | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Adjusted EBITDA more than doubled… achieved 8-9% margin target" (Feb 2026) | Revenue grew to $854M in fiscal 2025 (+11.8%); web-verified Q3-FY26 adjusted EBITDA $30.5M; the operating improvement is real | Matches — the operating turnaround is genuine |
| "Achieved positive net income… for the first time since 2021" (Nov 2025) | The multi-year trajectory is five straight net losses: -$44M (2021), -$7M, -$41M, -$21M, -$30M (2025). GAAP net margin -3.6%, return on equity -10.2%, return on invested capital -1.5% | Richer than the numbers — one clean quarter does not undo five years of GAAP losses; trailing diluted EPS is still -$0.30 |
| "Disciplined cost management… medical cost trend better than peers" | Gross margin 68.5% and expanding; the most credible operational claim, corroborated | Matches |
| "We're now generating consistent earnings and cash flow" (May 2026) | Trailing-twelve-month free cash flow is positive at $39M, but price-to-free-cash-flow is ~55x | Partly matches — the cash is real but the multiple prices in much more |
| Strong balance sheet enabling reinvestment | Verified net cash of about $45M (cash $139M vs total debt $94M) as of March 2026; solvency (Altman-Z 4.4) is sound | Matches — a genuine asset |

The most important divergence is not operational, it is on the bottom line and the price. The business is demonstrably better run than two years ago, but it still loses money on a generally-accepted-accounting basis, and the stock sits at 99% of its 52-week range and about 60% above its 200-day average — the market has already paid for the good news. The wider Q3-FY26 net loss (-$29.5M) was driven by $34.4 million of litigation accruals plus a $16.3 million vendor settlement, on top of a $27 million securities-fraud class-action settlement — a recurring reminder that this company is still working off the liabilities of its 2021-2022 crisis.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Rising, then maturing into measured.**

- May 2025: cautiously optimistic — "early progress," "growing confidence," guidance reaffirmed but not raised.
- Sep 2025: confident — "a year of delivery," guidance issued well above the prior year.
- Feb 2026: most confident point — hit the margin target "for the first time"; "we've pulled forward into two years what we thought was going to take three."
- May 2026: still positive but visibly hedging on the future — the language balances offense and defense, with explicit caution about "a more challenging rate environment for 2027" and a stated preference for "investing in growth while maintaining a consistent margin… more of a priority than expanding margins at this point." That sentence is a quiet signal that the easy margin gains are behind them.

The shift from "we will keep expanding margins" to "we will hold margins and reinvest" is the single most telling tonal move in the set.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**High.** This is the strongest part of the file. Management set a fiscal-2025 EBITDA bar of $31 million and delivered $34.5 million; set fiscal-2026 at $56-65 million and raised it twice to $85-90 million as results came in ahead. The screener's earnings-beat rate of 50% (three of six quarters) understates the pattern, because the misses were on the loss line while the operational guideposts (EBITDA, margin, census) were consistently met or exceeded. There is a mild sandbagging pattern — management repeatedly "assumes variability rather than relying on rate upside," then benefits when rates come in favorable. Reliability: High on the metrics they choose to guide; the open question is whether that credibility survives a genuinely adverse rate year.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

Analysts (Goldman Sachs, JPMorgan, and others) pushed repeatedly on three themes:

1. **Cost-of-care "geography."** Management has had to explain, call after call, that in-sourcing pharmacy and hospice shifts expenses between income-statement lines, making quarter-over-quarter cost trends look worse than the underlying. Legitimate, but a recurring opacity that makes the numbers harder to audit from outside.
2. **De novo (new-center) losses and time to break-even.** Management gives directional comfort but defers hard timelines ("we'll put out some guidance").
3. **The 2027 rate environment.** In May 2026, JPMorgan's Benjamin Rossi pressed on risk scores and acuity mix; management declined to commit, citing an in-progress budget process. This is the topic most likely to turn into bad news, and management is visibly not yet ready to address it.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🟢 Real, repeated operational delivery: EBITDA roughly tripled over the arc, margin target hit early, medical-cost discipline held while peers struggled (Feb 2026, May 2026).
🟢 Genuine net cash (~$45M) and sound solvency.
🟢 Insider conviction on the open market: 12 open-market buys (181,653 shares) versus 13 sells of just 70,005 shares — buyers committed far more capital than sellers.

🔴 Persistent senior-leadership churn: the chief medical officer left (May 2025), then the president/chief operating officer Michael Scarbrough departed "for personal reasons" one quarter later (Nov 2025). Management frames a "deep bench," but a transformation losing its operating leader is a real execution risk.
🔴 Recurring legal drag: a securities-fraud settlement ($27M) plus large litigation accruals and a vendor settlement that pushed the Q3-FY26 net loss wider — the past is still expensive.
🔴 The whole model rests on government reimbursement that management itself is flagging as a 2027 headwind.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

- The deliberate decision to **disenroll members who lost Medicaid eligibility** (Sep 2025) is the clearest sign management now prioritizes profit quality over headline census — a maturity signal, but also an admission that earlier growth carried lower-quality revenue.
- The language around CMS's calendar-2027 Medicare Advantage advance notice (Feb 2026) — "changes to Medicare Advantage policy do affect PACE," and a "blended risk score" that accelerates an unfavorable transition — is management pre-positioning investors for a softer rate year.
- New voices (chief medical officer Dr. Paul Taheri, chief administrative officer Meredith Delk) are pushing an AI-and-quality agenda; the candid "we're about 50% there" on care standardization reads as credible rather than promotional.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: STRENGTHENING operationally — but the value question is about price and terminal reimbursement, not execution.**

The single most important thing the director must weigh before sizing: the turnaround has already happened and the market has already paid for it. The stock is at the top of its range on the back of a margin target hit years early, while the forward driver management itself keeps flagging — the fiscal-2027 Medicaid and Medicare rate cycle — points the other way. Compounding this, roughly 70-75% of the shares are held by two private-equity sponsors (Apax and Welsh, Carson, Anderson & Stowe), who added two of their own directors in January 2026. That control block means there is no activist lever and no float-driven forced realization here; any value-unlock would come on the sponsors' timetable, not an outside investor's.

Moat: **NARROW**. InnovAge's advantage is a regulatory license (PACE is a tightly regulated, scarce program) plus integrated-care scale (it is the largest PACE operator). But the returns evidence does not support a wide moat: return on invested capital is still negative (-1.5%) and the company has only just reached generally-accepted profitability. A regulatory-license moat whose economics depend entirely on the government setting favorable rates is real but thin. Moat trend: **STABLE** — operations are improving the margin, but the rate-setting power sits with CMS and the states, not the company.

Secular threat: **MATERIAL** — reimbursement compression. This is not a technology-disruption story; it is the risk that legislated Medicaid cuts (the budget-reconciliation environment) and a less generous Medicare Advantage rate framework structurally compress the capitated rates that fund the entire model. Management's own 2027 caution is the tell. This is a dated, policy-driven risk on the same axis that pressures the broader government-funded healthcare cohort, not a terminal extinction — PACE enjoys bipartisan support and independent (MACPAC) validation — so it caps the upside rather than ending the story. The cheapness question is the crux: at 99% of its range and about 55 times free cash flow, the stock is not cheap, so this is neither a clear fear-print bargain nor an obvious value trap — it is a fairly-to-richly-priced good operator facing a known rate headwind.

CREDIBILITY_SCORE: 4 | TRAJECTORY: STRENGTHENING | MOAT: NARROW | MOAT_TREND: STABLE | SECULAR_THREAT: material
